results.title: Final Flow Survey of Langley 12-ft Low Speed Tunnel
results.abstract: A dynamic pressure calibration was conducted in the NASA Langley 12-Foot Low-Speed Tunnel for the final year of its operation. The objective was to calibrate the wall-mounted pitot static probe, used to measure freestream dynamic pressure during normal tunnel operations, relative to the dynamic pressure recorded over a cross-sectional area of the test section. The survey provided a calibration factor to be applied to the wall probe to accurately reflect an area weighted average of the air flow through the test section. Heat maps were also generated to visually show areas of the test section that airflow differs from the wall probe reading. This paper details the survey probe rake used and the methods for generating a calibration value for the tunnel as well as the implementation of that value. This calibration value serves as a correction factor that any testing in the tunnel would apply to the recorded data.

results.title: Development and Experimental Validation of a Path-Dependent Spin Forming Finite Element Model
results.abstract: Spin forming is an advanced manufacturing process widely used in the aerospace and defense sectors to produce lightweight, high-strength cylindrical components with tight dimensional tolerances. This study explores the applicability of the path-dependent Mechanical Threshold Stress (MTS) constitutive model by simulating the evolution of geometry, machining forces, and plastic deformation during the spin forming of a 10-mm thick 6061-O aluminum cylinder. While numerical modeling of spin forming has advanced substantially over the past decade, systematic verification and experimental validation of material models remain limited, particularly in predicting through-thickness process evolution. The MTS model, incorporating a Voce hardening rule, is employed for its ability to represent cyclic loading, rapidly varying temperature fields, and strain rates characteristic of spin forming. Numerical convergence analysis indicates discretization uncertainties between 0.3% and 9.2% for key quantities of interest. Experimental validation demonstrates that the MTS model, when implemented with a verified mesh, accurately reproduces both elastic and plastic behavior of 6061-O aluminum, predicting peak roller loads within 11–18% of measurements, geometric tolerances within 3%, and plastic strain distributions within 10% of experimental values. Collectively, these results establish a validated computational framework for predictive spin-forming simulations with quantified confidence, providing a foundation for extension to other alloys, geometries, and forming conditions.

results.title: System Identification of an Octocopter in Hover using Full-Harmonic Orthogonal Multisine Inputs
results.abstract: A new method for multi-input flight maneuver design for system identification is presented. The method consists of simultaneously injecting "full-harmonic'' orthogonal multisine signals into the flight control system. Orthogonality is achieved by repeating flight maneuvers with changing multisine polarities. The multisines can each contain the same frequency content, which can simplify frequency response estimation and can allow for a single flight maneuver designed using typical orthogonal multisine methods to be split into several shorter maneuvers, while maintaining the same frequency resolution and minimum frequency. Additionally, an input allocation scheme is presented that augments the multisines to size the vehicle response amplitude about a specific degree of freedom. To demonstrate the developed approach, flight testing was conducted with a small octocopter aircraft. The input allocation scheme was utilized successfully to increase excitation about the yaw axis, which often lacks control power for multirotor aircraft. Individual motor speeds and electrical power consumption measurements were recorded during flight and used to model the power and motor speed dynamics in addition to the rigid-body flight dynamics. The identified models are shown to predict the response of the vehicle and motor subsystems accurately. The models are parameterized primarily by individual rotor thrust and torque coefficients, which makes them suitable for analysis of both the aircraft flight dynamics and individual rotor aerodynamics. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that, for the small octocopter studied, the vehicle flight dynamics can be modeled accurately in near-hover conditions by neglecting rotor hub moments, variations in thrust and torque coefficients, gyroscopic moments in roll and pitch, and aerodynamic interaction effects.

results.title: Human Volunteer Lunar Landings While in a Standing Posture
results.abstract: INTRODUCTION Injury prediction and prevention while landing on the lunar surface in a standing configuration is an event with few analogs. Research on injury due to loading while standing unsupported has focused on pedestrians struck by automobiles. Vertical axis loading research has been conducted in the context of underbody blast injury (e.g., landmines), but this work is much higher rate and much more severe than a lunar landing. Additionally, lunar landings will involve restraints of some form to keep the crewmembers at their stations, potentially provide some offloading, and prevent the crewmember from impacting vehicle structures during the dynamic phases of flight. Terrestrial underbody loading involves a “preload” of gravity pushing the body into contact with the ground. In a lunar landing, the preload could range from a maximum of 1/6th Earth gravity as the vehicle’s thrusters act to slowly match the acceleration of the lunar surface to a minimum of no preload if the thrusters are turned off prior to landing, resulting in momentary free-fall prior to touchdown. Lunar landing while standing results in the ground accelerating towards the human. While the inverse case (human accelerating towards the ground) is similar, muscle activation strategies are likely different, resulting in different biomechanics. Human Landing System (HLS) providers are required to keep the dynamic response of a crewmember’s center of mass below injurious thresholds; however, there is currently no transfer function to predict the dynamic response of a standing occupant given the predicted vehicle accelerations. This work seeks to replicate lunar landing loads by dropping human volunteers on a human-rated test device while standing. The data collected will seek to overcome many of the limitations of the current NASA requirements governing crew landings while standing and address gaps relating to crew in dynamic environments. METHODS Human subjects will complete a series of tests utilizing the Vertical Deceleration Tower (VDT) at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base (WPAFB). The VDT consists of a carriage that is attached to a 60-foot guide rail system that allows for unpowered vertical drops. These tests will vary in peak acceleration, pulse length, landing angle, and by restraint and/or suit. The characterization of these variables have been determined by current NASA human standards and by characterization of realistic lunar landing conditions. Subjects will be outfitted with a full IMU (inertial measurement unit) suite and accelerometers to capture kinematic reactions to the drop tests. High speed video will capture additional kinematic data and load cells will capture the forces and moments at the feet and at the restraints. From the collected data, a post-test analysis of the subjects’ human performance will be performed. From this, a mathematical association between the probability of an unstable reaction and the input conditions will be created. This data will help inform appropriate levels of risk for lunar landings. The data collected from this study will also be delivered to other research efforts involving various computer-based modeling efforts, such as finite-element and musculoskeletal modeling. The proposed testing will generate data that can be used for standing landing model validation. This will include proper data filtering and necessary transformations of all applicable data collected. The study will also deliver a mass-spring-damper model similar to the Brinkley Dynamic Response Criterion (BDRC), a model currently used in part to certify space vehicles for transient accelerations experienced by seated crewmembers. The first part will include the natural frequency and damping coefficients in which the model is built on. The second part will include mapping the human performance analysis to the model to implement appropriate limits. Lastly, this study will provide a comparison analysis of unrestrained and restrained cases. This will include any statistical analyses of the effectiveness of restraints, recommendations for future efforts on the study of restraint effectiveness, and recommendations on how to implement deliverables into NASA in context of restraint use.

results.title: Computational Fluid Dynamics Analysis of Flame Dynamics in Partial Gravity Environments in a Rotating Centrifuge
results.abstract: The safety of spacecraft and crew members is a critical concern for space research and exploration missions. It is already known that fire hazards in a microgravity environment present unique challenges, primarily due to the absence of buoyancy, which significantly alters fire behavior. The NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to send humans to the Moon, introduces a new set of challenges due to the Moon partial gravity compared to the Earth. This necessitates a better understanding of fire behavior in partial gravity conditions. However, conducting experiments in true partial gravity environments is challenging, and the use of centrifuges to create artificial partial gravity introduces complications, including the Coriolis force and limitations in chamber size. Consequently, there have been limited studies on flame dynamics in partial gravity. To address these challenges, this research employs Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) techniques to investigate flame behavior in a partial gravity environment created by a rotating centrifuge. The numerical model is validated against NASA's previous experiments and provides information on the effects of the Coriolis force and flow recirculation in the chamber. The analysis reveals that the interaction between buoyancy, Coriolis force, and flow recirculation plays a significant role in flame behavior. The flame tilt angle observed in both the experiments and the numerical results is caused by the combined effects of these forces and their variations along the flame length. In conclusion, this research contributes to our understanding of how flames behave in partial gravity environments created by rotating centrifuges. It emphasizes the complexity of flame dynamics in such conditions and provides valuable insights for future centrifuge experiments, with the goal of improving space exploration safety and understanding flame behavior in unique partial gravity environment.

results.title: Pulsed Electroacoustic Analysis Capabilities at NASA Glenn Research Center
results.abstract: The High Voltage Testing Laboratory at NASA Glenn Research Center is equipped with a pulsed electroacoustic (PEA) analyzer to study space charge phenomena in dielectric materials. Dielectric materials such as those used in high voltage insulation systems are of great interest due to their crucial role in withstanding high voltages and avoiding electrical breakdown in electrified aircraft power systems. Current research is underway for the development of novel lightweight electrical insulation and the thorough evaluation of these materials is required. The PEA instrumentation at NASA GRC is a nondestructive method to evaluate the space charge phenomena which can give a unique insight on the feasibility and lifetime of material systems. The instrumentation capability and initial results are reported here.

results.title: Radar Performance Characterization Through Correlation with Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast from General Aviation
results.abstract: NASA Langley Research Center has several traffic sensors of various types installed around the center to monitor air traffic. These sensors help support beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) operations. In December 2024, NASA Langley Research Center D107 Simulation Development and Analysis Branch (SDAB) stood up a system to record data from all these sensors. To analyze the performance of these systems, a system of scripts was developed to accept recorded Radar and Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) data, correlate these datasets to each other, and measure the difference between the position of the aircraft as reported by the Radar system, and the ADS-B data recorded from the same aircraft. This enables analysis to see where the Radar systems provide adequate coverage of the airspace and where there may be areas of lower precision.

results.title: Measurement of Artificial and Real Bird Impact on a Very Rigid Flat Surface
results.abstract: Bird cadavers are used for development and certification testing of aircraft engines and structures to ensure that they can survive a bird strike during operation. The use of real birds has several disadvantages, including unsanitary test conditions, the need to euthanize animals, difficulty in procuring birds of the correct mass and species at arbitrary times of the year, and variability in test results due to bird-to-bird differences and the difficulty in launching an irregularly shaped projectile in a repeatable manner. Artificial bird projectiles could overcome many of the disadvantages of real birds and may be acceptable to designers and certification authorities if they can be shown to produce a similar response to that of real birds. This has led to the investigation of artificial bird materials that can be used in lieu of real birds that would produce the same damage and response in aircraft structures as real birds.

results.title: Need for Portable Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Navigation Solutions
results.abstract: In the Artemis campaign, as astronauts venture farther from their lander than ever before, reliable surface navigation becomes essential, particularly in contingency scenarios. Early missions will rely on traditional orienteering methods supported by tools such as a sun compass. To safely expand surface mobility while minimizing navigation workload, a portable suit system is needed to provide position, navigation, and timing (PNT) services using in-situ resources.

results.title: Egress Fitness
results.abstract:
The transition between gravity environments is one of the most complex, high-risk phases of exploration missions. The reduced functional capacity caused by physiological deconditioning and adaptations in microgravity coupled with the stressors of re-entry into gravity environments will increase the risk to crew, even with rigorous adherence to inflight countermeasures. Specifically, two high-risk scenarios may be required to be performed soon after gravity transitions: 1) nominal and/or emergency unassisted capsule egress task after return to Earth, and 2) planetary extravehicular activity (EVA) soon after landing on Mars or the Moon. Quantification of functional performance after exposure to extended durations in microgravity is necessary to inform concepts of operations and contingency scenarios for future exploration missions.

The overarching aim of this study is to quantify post-landing functional performance in crewmembers with physiological deconditioning after long-duration missions on the International Space Station (ISS). This study has two phases. Phase 1 includes a pilot study to assess the overall feasibility and demonstrate the capability to perform mission-like tasks shortly after landing from an ISS mission. Phase 2, the Egress Fitness study, which is part of the Complement of Integrated Protocols for Human Exploration Research (CIPHER), uses a task-based approach to characterize functional performance in long-duration ISS crewmembers before flight and shortly after return to Earth. The pilot and full Egress Fitness study includes pre-flight and post-flight testing of simulated emergency egress out of a functional capsule mockup and a high-fidelity Mars gravity EVA simulation at the Active Response Gravity Offload System (ARGOS) facility. The EVA simulation tasks include suit donning, hatch egress, ladder descent, task board cable operations, baggage transfer over sand/rocky regolith, traverse, geological sampling, alignment with a rear entry port, and suit egress (with the Pilot study including a subset of the EVA tasks). The post-flight simulated capsule egress test occurs 1–4 h after landing and the planetary EVA simulation occurs 18–36 h after landing. The full CIPHER Egress Fitness study included post-flight sessions on R+1, 4, and 8 to characterize the timeframe of recovery. 

In 2025, four private astronauts on a 3.5-day commercial orbital mission completed capsule egress, both from their actual flight capsule and the capsule mockup. Results showed a greater change in time to completion for the actual capsule egress compared to the mockup capsule egress, indicating improved sensorimotor function in as little as three hours after landing. 

CIPHER Egress Fitness has completed three subjects in full, 1 subject with capsule egress only and has 3 subjects currently in progress. This study will quantify post-landing functional performance in operationally relevant simulations to help inform fitness for duty standards and future planetary concepts of operations shortly after landing.

results.title: Rediscovering Apollo Biomedical Data to Support Artemis: The Synthesis of Apollo-Era Records Project (SOAR)
results.abstract: With the first crewed missions of the Artemis Program on the horizon, including the return of humans to another planetary surface, the space medicine and research communities have a renewed interest in using data collected during the Apollo program to buy down risk. Archivists with NASA’s Life Sciences Data Archive (LSDA) and epidemiologists with the Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH) are responding to the increasing number of Apollo-related data requests by collaborating on the Synthesis Of Apollo-era Records (SOAR) Project, which seeks to fulfill this interest by expanding the available historic biomedical knowledge base. The SOAR team is examining physical records located across a wide range of collections, including records such as pre-flight and post-flight physicals, lab reports, and handwritten flight surgeon and biomedical engineer console logs from the Apollo missions. The SOAR team have identified, inventoried, and started to digitize several sources of Apollo-era biomedical information. In addition, the team is experimenting with using AI tools to extract the data from scanned documents and present them in formats suitable for analysis and reuse. This presentation will discuss the progress of the project, give context to the dual research-clinical care nature of the records, and highlight the challenges and opportunities in using data from historical records. This presentation will also provide information on how researchers can request access to datasets from these records.

results.title: Diverse organic molecules on Mars revealed by the first SAM TMAH experiment

organization.name: Laboratoire Réactions et Génie des Procédés

results.abstract: The search for organic matter on Mars has rapidly evolved in the past decade with simple aromatic, S-heterocycles, and aliphatic organic molecules detected in Gale crater. We report the in situ detection of >20 organic molecules from clay-bearing sandstones in the ~3.5-billion-year-old Knockfarrill Hill member of Glen Torridon, Gale crater, by the Sample Analysis at Mars instrument suite onboard the Curiosity rover. These molecules were liberated by the onboard tetramethylammonium hydroxide wet chemistry experiment. Diverse thermochemolysis products, including benzothiophene, methyl benzoate, and single and dicyclic aromatic molecules were released and detected by evolved gas analysis and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Results indicate the experiment successfully released molecules preserved in ancient macromolecular or free organic matter within Martian bedrock despite ~3.5 billion years of diagenesis and radiation exposure.

results.title: Predicting Spaceflight Operational Performance From Sensorimotor Assessment Tasks
results.abstract: INTRODUCTION Exploration class missions will require a new level of crew autonomy to self-assess and treat their sensorimotor dysfunction around periods of gravitational transition, where sensorimotor disturbances are at their highest. A sensorimotor assessment task set was developed to assess performance capabilities prior to early extravehicular activities (EVAs) based on lessons learned from Apollo and through feedback from subject matter experts. The task set included the following requirements: 1) mimic body maneuvers that would be performed during an EVA such that crew can self-assess their potential ability to complete operational tasks; 2) provide opportunities to develop strategies to recover from off-nominal body positions; and 3) aid in progressive adaptation to the novel gravitational environment. The purpose of this study was to validate the task set using a sensorimotor spaceflight analog to induce varying levels of disruption including the Sensorimotor Disorientation Analog (SDA) [1]. METHODS Forty-one healthy non-astronaut subjects (21 males, 20 females; Mean ± SD, Age: 34.0 ± 7.8 years) participated. Subjects attended two testing sessions: 1) familiarization to the tasks and baseline data collection, and 2) tasks completed under two levels of sensorimotor disorientation mimicking astronaut postflight performance at R+0 and R+1. Subjects performed a series of seven sensorimotor assessment tasks followed by two operationally relevant EVA analog tasks. The sensorimotor assessments tasks, ordered from least to most provocative of the sensorimotor system, included: postural stability, step test, prone & supine recovery from fall (RFF), four-square-step-test, obstacle negotiation with turns (OTT), kneel-and-reach. Operational analog tasks included a top-hatch capsule egress and a 5-minute EVA traversal. Disorientation was applied using galvanic vestibular stimulation and weighted trunk, wrists, and ankles. RESULTS Pearsons’ correlation r-values were calculated between 1) all assessment tasks and 2) each assessment and operational analog task, across individuals and SDA levels (n=120). Strong correlations were present between each assessment task (r ≥ 0.59). The two assessment tasks with the strongest correlations to the operational analog tasks were the RFF (r ≥ 0.45) and OTT (r ≥ 0.60). To assess the ability of the sensorimotor tasks to predict operational analog task performance and aid in task down-selection, leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) was conducted with a linear model of assessment tasks selected using stepwise regression. The operational analog predictors were the time to complete the top-hatch capsule egress and the number of bag transfers complete during the 5-minute EVA traversal. For capsule egress, only the OTT was included in the model with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 12.8 sec between predicted and observed values (Q2 = 0.35). For the EVA traversal, the RFF, OTT, and FSST were included in the model with an MAE of 6.5 bags (Q2 = 0.53). DISCUSSION These results provide early evidence for the down-selection of assessment tasks that were best able to predict performance in operationally relevant tasks for use in upcoming Artemis missions. ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS This project is funded by the NASA Human Research Program.

results.title: Ground Slope Effects on Lander Radiator Performance
results.abstract: Two sensitivity studies were performed to examine the drop in radiator heat rejection from slopes. Study #1 used a 5.5m tall reduced order asset to represent a small-lander/rover. Study #2 used a 20m asset represent a tall lander. The assets had body mounted horizontal, 45º inward-tilted, and vertical radiator orientations. The impact of slopes on different radiator orientations and on radiators pointing different directions (i.e., slope verses sun) was investigated. The studies were conducted at a polar location of -82.5ºS to capture the incident solar flux at the northmost, and therefore the hottest, range of potential Artemis landing sites (Mons Mouton Plateau).

results.title: Summary Results From the Assessment of Psychology in Extreme Environments (APEX) Standardized Suite
results.abstract: BACKGROUND Future space exploration missions to the Moon and Mars will require small teams of astronauts to work and live in an extreme circumstance including long-term isolation and confinement. While there has been extensive research in space and space analog settings, the characterization of behavioral health, interpersonal relationships, team functioning, and performance has been difficult due to small sample sizes. To address this, we administered and iteratively refined a standard suite of measures called the Assessment of Psychology in Extreme Environments (APEX) Suite to individuals and teams in isolation and used this data to characterize key behavioral health, team and performance risks over time. METHOD Data were collected with the APEX Suite on 121 individuals in 40 teams, each consisting of 3 to 9 members living and working in isolation and confinement. The sample included astronauts in space for 150-350 days, and in terrestrial analogs from 45-240 days. The APEX Suite included a set of validated self-report measures, performance tests, and physiological biomarkers that quantify individual and team-level responses to the conditions expected for individuals and teams operating in long-duration, extreme environments. Data were harmonized across settings, allowing for analyses. RESULTS We will present results examining key behavioral health, interpersonal relationships, team functioning and performance metrics over time in isolation, as well as a comparison of astronauts on the International Space Station with research analog astronauts. Example results include no incidents of clinically elevated depression across the sample. For affect and stress, some temporal trends were observed, including a decrease in positive affect over time; however, negative affect and stress showed substantial interindividual variability and appeared to be more strongly associated with situational stressors than with duration in isolation. DISCUSSION We will discuss the implications of our results for informing and prioritizing countermeasures for future exploration missions. We also will describe how research and operations can leverage the APEX Suite to test the effectiveness of countermeasures in small samples and prepare for future exploration-class missions.

results.title: Towards Early Design Modeling and Simulation of Distributed Situation Awareness
results.abstract: Human operators play a major role in maintaining the safety of complex systems. While operator error is a major cause of hazardous events, operators also contribute to resilience by preventing, mitigating, and recovering from hazardous events. A key factor underlying this resilience is situation awareness–the ability of operators to understand their environment and each other to achieve desired system functions. This remains true for fully and partially-autonomous systems, where operational responsibility is shared with designed technical functionality that also relies on (a form of) situation awareness to conduct operations. Distributed Situation Awareness (DSA) theory, which defines situation awareness as a system property, is best suited to represent situation awareness in systems that share situation awareness properties among (human and non-human) agents.This work proposes a framework to computationally simulate DSA to enable the study operational resilience in complex engineered systems. Specifically, this framework enables the modeling of hazardous scenarios related to DSA in an integrated behavioral simulation. This approach advances existing DSA modeling approaches, which analyze situation awareness-related constructs alone, by enabling the analysis of the dynamic interactions between DSA-related constructs and other system elements (e.g., software glitches, human error, etc.) and their effects on overall system behavior. This framework is demonstrated using aircraft taxiway example, where it is used to model taxiing conflicts arising due to lack of vision and poor communications from the air traffic controller. This demonstration shows the potential of using simulations to understand DSA-related hazards and thus inform the design of resilience.

results.title: In-Space Demonstration of Spray-on Solar White Paint
results.abstract: Discs coated with spray-on solar white and two similar thermal control coatings were flown in low earth orbit for roughly five hours. While in orbit, the coated discs were exposed to direct sunlight and to deep space for short intervals. Measurements of disc temperatures showed that the spray-on solar white coating had the lowest absorption of sunlight. Numerical modeling was used to infer that spray-on solar white had a solar absorptance between 0.02 and 0.04 and a thermal emittance between 0.93 and 0.99, both of which are consistent with terrestrial laboratory measurements.

results.title: General Services Administration Reclamation Yard Solid Waste Management Unit #010 2025 Groundwater Monitoring Report Kennedy Space Center, Florida
results.abstract:
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), through its Environmental Assurance Branch, is managing cleanup of two areas at the General Services Administration Reclamation Yard (GSRY) at John F. Kennedy Space Center (KSC), Florida. The area located in the northeast portion of the GSRY has historically been referred to as the Northeast Area and Polychlorinated Biphenyl (PCB)/Volatile Organic Aromatic Plume. The area located in the western portion of the GSRY has historically been referred to as the Southwest Area, Southwest Hot Spot, and Chlorinated Volatile Organic Compound (VOC) Plume. The GSRY has been designated Solid Waste Management Unit (SWMU) #010 under KSC’s Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) Corrective Action Program.  This report was prepared by Jacobs Geosyntec, a Joint Venture (JGJV) under contract 80KSC024DA004, Task Order 80KSC024FA115.

The contaminants of concern (COCs) for the Northeast Area consist of PCBs, 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene, and breakdown products of 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene.  Groundwater results demonstrate a reduction in plume size and COC concentrations compared to baseline sampling for the 2018 interim measure (IM).  Chlorinated benzene compound COCs were detected above State of Florida Groundwater Cleanup Target Levels (GCTLs) in the 10 to 30 ft BLS interval only.  The VOC plume is delineated, both horizontally and vertically.  There were no detections of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).  Iron, manganese, sodium and total dissolved solids (TDS) are monitored at select locations in compliance with underground injection control (UIC) requirements.  The results indicated that concentrations of one or more of these analytes is above the site-approved screening level in each of the three UIC monitoring wells.  It is recommended that PCB analysis be discontinued based on more than two consecutive results below the GCTL.  Monitoring for VOCs and for the UIC parameters is recommended to continue on an annual basis.

Annual UIC monitoring was conducted in the Southwest Area at three monitoring wells. Concentrations of iron and TDS remain above the site-approved screening levels in two of the three  monitoring wells sampled.  It is recommended that groundwater monitoring continue on an annual basis for iron and TDS.

Analytical Calculation of the Dose to an Ellipsoidal Target By Energetic Ions
results.abstract: The energy deposited in small targets by ionizing radiation is a fundamental quantity necessary for the understanding of the biological effect of ionizing radiation. In recent work, we have calculated the energy deposited in a spherical target by an ion track as a function of the impact parameter using amorphous track models, the Local Effect Model and the Kieffer-Chatterjee Model. In this work, the calculation is performed for an ellipsoid. The calculation is more difficult due to the lack of symmetry and more parameters needed to describe the situation. The analytical calculations were compared with simulations performed using the radiation track structure code RITRACKS (Relativistic Ion Tracks) using six ions of interest in space radiation (<sup>1</sup>H<sup>+</sup>, 1,000 MeV; <sup>4</sup>He<sup>2+</sup>, 250 MeV/n; <sup>12</sup>C<sup>6+</sup>, 290 MeV/n; <sup>16</sup>O<sup>8+</sup>, 325 MeV/n; <sup>28</sup>Si<sup>14+</sup>, 300 MeV/n; <sup>56</sup>Fe<sup>26+</sup>, 1,000 MeV/n). For tracks intersecting the targets directly, the difference between the model and the simulations with RITRACKS is about 3% or less. For tracks not intersecting the target, the difference is over 100 %, but the trends as a function of the distance are similar. These calculations are important because many cell nuclei have an ellipsoid shape and provide a simple alternative to Monte-Carlo track structure calculations, especially for irradiation by microbeams and in tissue models. To the author’s knowledge, this model is the only one that can do dose calculation in an ellipsoid target from ion tracks using a simple mathematical equation.

results.title: Electron Velocity Moments in the Solar Wind. I. Calibration of the Wind 3DP EESA Low Detector
results.abstract: Calibrated measurements of electron velocity distribution functions (VDFs) are necessary to characterize fluid and kinetic processes in weakly collisional and nearly collisionless plasmas such as the solar wind. Therefore, we analyzed 3,996,051 electron VDFs observed by the Wind 3DP thermal electron detector near 1 astronomical unit (au) between January 1, 2005 and November 25, 2017. The data were calibrated for each electron VDF to produce accurate velocity moments in the solar wind. This is the first full solar cycle coverage electron velocity moment dataset in the near-Earth solar wind. Herein (Paper I) we discuss the calibration process/algorithms and the velocity moment constraints, uncertainties, and resulting public dataset. In the second paper (Paper II), we statistically analyze the electron velocity moment dataset.

results.title: Characteristics of Tropospheric Clouds over Dome C, Antarctica, using CALIPSO and In-situ Measurements
results.abstract: This study characterizes the behavior of single-layer tropospheric clouds over Dome C, Antarctica, using satellite observations from Cloud-Aerosol Lidar and Infrared Pathfinder Satellite Observation (CALIPSO), in-situ radiosonde profiles, surface measurements, and large-scale meteorological fields from reanalyses for a three-year period (April 2009 to March 2012). The vertical structure, distribution, and thermodynamic environment of different cloud types are examined, including the most significant cloud properties that influence the surface downwelling longwave radiation. Dome C generally features clouds with low cloud base (88% occurrence frequency), which are thicker during winter and fall forming due to the advection of warm and moist oceanic airmass deep into the continent. Conversely, low, thin clouds forming by saturation of local air rising and cooling are prevalent during spring and summer. Clouds are mainly composed of ice except during November to February when thin, low liquid-containing clouds are routinely observed (37% occurrence frequency). All cloud types enhance downwelling longwave radiation compared to clear skies. The major factor influencing surface longwave radiation impact is cloud thickness for ice-only clouds whereas is cloud optical depth for liquid-containing clouds. The longwave impact of clouds with super-cooled liquid water depends mainly on cloud microphysics as opposed to cloud geometry. Analysis of cloud temperature profiles show that low and mid-level clouds are mostly warmer than surface, a feature important for passive cloud remote sensing. These results provide insights on cloud characteristics over the interior Antarctic Plateau, exploring their influence on surface radiation budget and highlighting the need for additional cloud microphysical observations.

results.title: Desert Dust Exerts Twice the Longwave Radiative Heating Estimated By Climate Models

organization.name: Laboratoire des Sciences du Climat et de l'Environnement
Laboratoire des Sciences du Climat et de l'Environnement
Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology

results.abstract: Although desert dust is the most abundant atmospheric aerosol by mass, its longwave radiative effects remain unclear, obscuring the impacts of dust on weather and climate. Here, using a data-driven analytical model constrained by observations, we show that scattering and absorption of longwave radiation by dust heats the planet by +0.25 ± 0.06 W m⁻² (90% confidence). This is nearly twice the value simulated by current climate models, which omit longwave scattering and underrepresent super coarse dust (diameter > 10 μm). These omissions bias modeled surface energy fluxes, cloud responses, precipitation, and atmospheric circulation. At the global scale, the sign and magnitude of the net dust direct radiative effect remain uncertain, with additional work needed to constrain shortwave cooling effects. These findings show that improving the representation of dust interactions with longwave radiation can improve weather forecasting and is essential to resolve the role of dust in climate change.

results.title: Bilayered Martian Polar CO2 Snow Generation

organization.name: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory

results.abstract: The exchange of CO2 between the atmosphere and the polar ice caps is a fundamental 11 process on Mars, for both present-day and past climates, affecting the dynamics of the 12 atmosphere and other surface-atmosphere interactions across the globe. Recent observations 13 have shown multiple spatial-temporal variations in the atmosphere-surface CO2 exchange in 14 polar regions, including seasonal and interannual, longitudinal, and hemispheric variations. The 15 causes of these variations remain uncertain. We examine the spatial-temporal variations of snow 16 generation, and its connections to dynamical processes, using Mars Weather Research and 17 Forecasting model (MarsWRF) simulations. The simulations indicate that there are two separable 18 vertical layers of CO2 snow formation: a thin near-surface layer and a broader upper layer 19 between 300 and 10 Pa. The snow generation in the upper layer is confined to high latitudes and 20 occurs in subregions within the cold areas inside the polar vortex, whereas the near-surface snow 21 is generated further equatorward and extends as far as the seasonal snow cap. While the two 22 separate layers are directly connected to different dynamical processes (baroclinic waves in the 23 near-surface layer and polar vortex dynamics in the upper layer) there are indicators of coupling 24 between the layers. The same waves appear in both layers, with strong lag correlations, and the 25 two layers are associated with the thermally indirect Ferrel cell poleward of the winter polar 26 vortex edge.

results.title: Global Retrieval Dataset of UV-VIS Extinction and Absorption of Above-cloud Aerosols from Synergy of A-train Active-Passive measurements: Part I—Above-cloud Aerosol Optical Depth from CALIOP Depolarization Ratio Method
results.abstract: We present the global above-cloud aerosol optical depth (ACAOD) retrieval dataset derived using the Depolarization Ratio (DR) method applied to CALIOP cloudy-sky measurements. The DR method was among the first lidar-based remote sensing technique to quantify the aerosol loading over clouds without involving any specific assumptions about detailed vertical profiles of aerosols and their optical-microphysical properties, except for the lidar ratio of the cloud layer. Physically based on the two-way transmission of lidar signal, the DR method uses 1) layer-integrated attenuated backscatter at 532 nm, γ'<sub>532</sub>, and 2) layer-integrated attenuated depolarization ratio at 532 nm, δ'<sub>532</sub>, to deduce the optical depth of aerosols above opaque water clouds (OWCs) at 532 nm. First, we derived a global climatology of calibration constant, γ'<sun>water, unobstructed</sub>, which represents the layer-integrated attenuated backscatter of the unobstructed water clouds. Second, we applied the DR method with an optimal configuration using the CALIOP Level 2 cloud and aerosol layer products to derive ACAOD dataset globally. Third, we validate the retrieved ACAOD against the direct airborne measurements acquired from HSRL-2 lidar and 4STAR sun photometer operated during the ORACLES field campaign in 2016-2018 over the southeastern Atlantic Ocean. DR ACAOD correlates well (R<sup>2</sup>~0.95 for HSRL-2 and R<sup>2</sup> ~0.75 for 4STAR) against airborne measurements, however, with an overall positive bias of ~0.088. An inter-satellite comparison of CALIOP-retrieved ACAOD against the research dataset derived from Aqua-MODIS over the southeastern Atlantic Ocean show a good-level of agreement, whereas the operational retrievals from OMI were found to show a negative bias of ~0.13. The Extinction Ångström Exponent derived from the combination of DR method ACAOD and color ratio of 1064-532 nm provided the known regional distribution of fine-mode carbonaceous smoke and coarse-mode mineral dust aerosols. We also calculated the above-cloud aerosol lidar ratio from the derived extinction optical depth and backscatter measurements. The global dataset of reliable ACAOD from CALIOP paves the way for a potential synergy with NASA's A-train sensors, such as OMI and MODIS, for constraining the UV-VIS observations to derive spectral aerosol absorption properties over clouds, which are essential for estimating direct and semi-direct radiative effects of aerosols in cloudy atmospheres.

results.title: Thermal Performance of Common Bulk-Fill Cryogenic Insulation Materials in Helium and Hydrogen Background Gases
results.abstract: Maritime shipping of vast quantities of liquid hydrogen (LH<sub>2</sub>) will be necessary to facilitate a global hydrogen ecosystem; with some studies estimating volumes up to 172,000 m<sup>3</sup> for individual tanker ships, and requiring stationary storage tanks at terminals of 50,000 m<sup>3</sup> to 100,000 m<sup>3</sup>—ten to fifteen times larger than the current largest tank, located at launch pad B at NASA Kennedy Space Center (KSC).  Such a radical scale-up will push the boundary of traditional, vacuum-insulated tank designs.  Hence, a potential need exists for non-vacuum solutions, which necessitates exploring the thermal performance of insulation materials in non-condensable background gasses at LH<sub>2</sub> temperatures, namely helium and hydrogen.  Testing of two bulk-fill insulation materials common to large LH<sub>2</sub> storage tanks, perlite and glass bubbles, in helium and hydrogen was recently conducted by the Cryogenics Test Laboratory at KSC using the Cryostat-100 liquid nitrogen boiloff calorimeter per the ASTM C1774 standard methodology.  Effective thermal conductivity (k<sub>e</sub>) and heat flux (q) results for each insulation/gas combination are presented across the full vacuum range, as well as thermal profiles through the insulation thickness between 78 K and 293 K.

results.title: Towards an improved understanding of the Antarctic coastal zone and its contribution to future global sea level

organization.name: National Institute of Oceanography and Applied Geophysics
National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research
Alfred-Wegener-Institut Helmholtz-Zentrum für Polar- und Meeresforschung
Alfred-Wegener-Institut Helmholtz-Zentrum für Polar- und Meeresforschung
Alfred Wegener Institute Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research

results.abstract: Understanding the coastal zone of the Antarctic Ice Sheet, where it interacts with the Southern Ocean and warmer air masses, is crucial for predicting Antarctica's influence on the global climate. This region has multiple tipping mechanisms that could trigger large, rapid, and potentially irreversible changes in the coming centuries. The Antarctic Ice Sheet remains the largest source of uncertainty in future sea-level projections. Insufficient knowledge of bed topography beneath the ice shelves and the coastal ice sheet is not yet well documented, but is a major source of this uncertainty. This review assesses current knowledge of the coastal zone and highlights methods to investigate it, including aerogeophysical surveys, ground- and ship-based measurements, satellite observations, and computer modeling. An ensemble analysis of published bed topography datasets identifies significant data gaps and their regional distribution, framed in the context of current ice-sheet behavior and potential instability. We propose scientific priorities and guidelines for future aerogeophysical surveys, advocating for a comprehensive, coordinated international effort to build a next-generation dataset of Antarctic bed properties. Such an initiative would significantly advance understanding of the role of coastal processes in ice-sheet dynamics, reducing uncertainties in sea-level rise projections and enhancing predictions of future ocean and climate changes.

results.title: Is Constitutive Red-Shift an Advantage for Oxygenic Photosynthesis Under M-Dwarf Starlight? Insights From Acaryochloris Marina Sp. Str. Moss Beach
results.abstract: In the next years, several space missions will search for evidence of life on exoplanets, focusing on robust biosignatures associated with oxygenic photosynthesis, including atmospheric oxygen accumulation and the Vegetation Red-Edge in surface reflectance spectra. Many potentially habitable rocky exoplanets orbit M-dwarf stars, whose spectral energy distribution may challenge oxygenic photosynthesis. Differently from the Sun, M-dwarf stars emit predominantly far-red (700– 750 nm) and infrared (750–1000 nm) light, and relatively little visible (400–700 nm) radiation, which constitutes photosynthetically active radiation. Some organisms have been found to photosynthesize under such spectrum but less efficiently than under solar light, as their photosynthetic apparatus evolved to harvest visible light emitted by the Sun. Around M-dwarfs, such different irradiation might have selected adaptations optimized for harvesting far-red / infra-red light. On Earth, similar selection can be found in Acaryochloris marina strains, constitutively presenting high chlorophyll d content in photosystem II & I, with in vivo absorption peaks beyond 700 nm. Here we tested the Moss Beach strain under a simulated M-dwarf spectrum and a simulated primeval atmosphere – anoxic and enriched in carbon dioxide. Results underline how this permanently red-shifted photosynthetic apparatus does not require acclimation to the stellar spectrum and enables for a strong growth and oxygen production, higher than under simulated solar light. Moreover, cells’ reflectance spectrum highlights a shift of the canonical red-edge toward longer wavelengths, resulting in a Chl d-near-infrared edge, suggesting a similar metabolism on exoplanets orbiting M-dwarfs could successfully produce both a gaseous biosignature and a characteristic surface biosignature.

results.title: Robotic Infrastructure Construction and Maintenance Systems for the Moon, Mars, and Other Missions
results.abstract:
Building infrastructure in the extreme environments of space is exceptionally challenging, creating a need for lightweight, durable, economic, and remotely deployable initial infrastructure to pave the way for future activities on the Moon and Mars. Autonomous construction systems will be necessary to develop infrastructure in the remote and extreme environments encountered in space exploration. The NASA ARMADAS system of autonomously assembled modular structures presents the opportunity for building infrastructure that is both suited to transportation constraints and mission adaptive through inherent reconfigurability. NASA and M3 are developing the capabilities and near-term application of this system towards a deployment-ready solution for in-space infrastructure development. 

This work and similar projects will become the foundation for robotic construction standards, illustrating that this can be scaled from modest to immense structures. This work will also increase domain knowledge of commercial and flight specific robotic design requirements for system integration with in-space manufacturing and sustainable massless space exploration goals.

results.title: Initiating Cartographic Standards for Artemis III Map Products Used By Crew and Flight Control Team
results.abstract: The Artemis missions are reintroducing the need for spatial data products to plan, train, and execute mission objectives for the lunar surface. Spatial data products were used during the Apollo era across the entire mission life cycle, including identification of landing sites, tracking of orbital paths across the lunar surface in Apollo Mission Control, and execution of surface extravehicular activity (EVA) traverses and stations. In the decades since, the transition of NASA’s human spaceflight focus to the Shuttle program and the International Space Station (ISS) has caused the stagnation in use of planetary spatial data beyond the Earth. The most recent spatial data products for crewed lunar activities were created in the 1970’s and have become outdated due to significant advances in lunar dataset volume and diversity, digital geographic information system (GIS) capabilities, and cartographic standards that have evolved to leverage GIS capabilities to answer novel problems. Therefore, the Analysis & Mapping for Planetary Exploration and Science (AMPES) team at NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) is seeking to modernize NASA’s cartographic standards for spatial data products that are specific to surface-scale lunar activities to be responsive to the operational needs of crewed Artemis missions.

results.title: 81 GHz UAS Traffic Management Via ADS-B
results.abstract: This paper explores the feasibility of using millimeter-wave to broadcast Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) at (81 GHz +/- 50 MHz) to support Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS) Traffic Management (UTM) functions such as detect-and-avoid and short-range traffic coordination in high-density, time-critical operations. Using FLARM-based avionics as the message source, we implement an up/down-conversion architecture that translates FLARM/ADS-B flight information onto a W-band frequency channel, evaluate performance with shared and independent local oscillators, and integrate custom antennas with off-the-shelf power amplifiers to assess link reliability. The bench testing demonstrates stable conversion under controlled conditions, while initial outdoor over-the-air trials characterize signal detection performance and phase-noise sensitivities. Planned open-air tests at NASA’s Armstrong Test Facility and flight demonstrations at NASA Langley will quantify operational range and explore the suitability of W-band ADS-B for localized, low-interference airspace services in next-generation UTM.

results.title: Dust Mitigation Technology Roadmap: LSIC Spring 2026
results.abstract: As humans return to the Moon and set their sites on Mars with spacesuits, rovers, habitats, and other assets during the Artemis missions, the lunar and Martian regolith (i.e. dust) covering the surface will be an environmental and performance challenge to nominal and contingency operations. Accounts from Apollo astronauts and analysis of hardware returned from the surface illustrate just how deleterious the dust can be.  During Apollo missions, the lunar dust adhered to the spacesuits mechanically and electrostatically, and the rovers experienced mechanical malfunctions. The Exploration Systems Development Mission Directorate (ESDMD) defines and manages systems development for programs critical to NASA’s Artemis program and planning for NASA’s Moon to Mars (M2M) exploration approach. ESDMD manages the human exploration system development for lunar orbital, lunar surface, and Mars exploration.

results.title: Hydrocarbon Burn Facility, SWMU 007, Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances Pilot Study Implementation Work Plan, Kennedy Space Center, Florida
results.abstract:
This Pilot Study Implementation Work Plan (IWP) details the pilot study design to reduce per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) migration within surface water at the Hydrocarbon Burn Facility (HBF) remediation site. Objectives of the pilot study are to reduce PFAS loading to surface water features at HBF and the Banana River. Pilot study design includes the use of sorbent matting and barriers. The IWP builds on the design from the Remedial Alternatives Evaluation presented to the KSC Remediation Team in December 2024.

The remedial technology for the pilot study will consist of sorbent matting to line surface water channels to prevent contamination in groundwater from migrating to surface water, and filter bags containing sorbent media to remove contaminants in the surface water. The matting product to be used is CETCO’s REACTIVE CORE MAT®, which is filled with FLUORO-SORB® 200. FLUORO-SORB® adsorbent is a proprietary, surface-modified granular clay media that has been proven to effectively treat PFAS in a variety of removal and remediation applications. The treatment barriers will be set up along the surface water channels using filter bags filled with Hydrosil’s HS-ACC granular activated carbon, to treat PFAS already in surface water. The filter bags will be contained in gabion baskets that are secured along the surface water channels. 

Sorbent materials will be placed in two separate areas for the pilot study. Pilot Study Area #1 is a surface water channel located along Static Test Road. PFAS concentrations in this location are less than in surface water features closer to the main HBF area, but the surface water in this location flows directly to the Banana River.  Pilot Study Area #2 is a low-lying area closer to the main HBF area where higher PFAS concentrations in groundwater and surface water are present. Pilot Study installation and implementation is planned for later this year.

results.title: NASA Science Mission Directorate’s Strategy for Data Management and Computing to Accelerate Scientific Discovery 2025–2030
results.abstract: NASA's Science Mission Directorate (SMD) seeks to “discover the secrets of the universe, to search for life elsewhere in the Universe, and to protect and improve life on Earth and in space” (NASA, 2025). To achieve these ambitious exploration goals, SMD manages its scientific data infrastructure and provides high-end computing (HEC) capabilities that support NASA's entire mission portfolio. These capabilities inform critical decision-making across multiple areas of national importance: precision agriculture support that safeguards our food supplies, space weather predictions for protecting critical infrastructure, and advanced simulations for rocket development. From Mars mission simulations to deep space data processing, this infrastructure advances our understanding of Earth, our solar system, and the universe beyond while pushing the boundaries of human exploration. SMD continuously prioritizes the development and evolution of these systems so that they continue to enable breakthrough discoveries and deliver direct benefits to the American people.

results.title: Recommended Practice for Use of ExB Probes in Electric Propulsion Testing
results.abstract: An ExB probe is an electric propulsion plume diagnostic that has at its core a Wien filter.  Ions entering the instrument experience perpendicular electric and magnetic fields and are filtered based on their velocity. While the ExB probe can be used to estimate the ion velocity distribution function, in the electric propulsion community, it is commonly used to measure species fractions.  There are numerous probe designs, implementation and operation procedures, and data analysis approaches described and in use across the community.  This paper provides recommendations and descriptions of best practices for design, implementation, and data analysis for the ExB probe, with a particular emphasis on Hall and ion thrusters.  This work contributes to the broader community goal to standardize the use of diagnostics in electric propulsion testing.

results.title: GVIPS Prediction of Cyclic Ratchetting Behavior and Cycles with Interrupted Relaxation Periods of TIMETAL 21S at 650 °C
results.abstract: The predictive performance of a multimechanism GVIPS model with saturating hardening function is assessed against a set of high temperature cyclic experiments under both strain-control and stress-control at varying rates of loading as well as several complex interrupted cyclic responses. The material specimens were composed of the titanium alloy, TIMETAL 21S, and tested at 650 °C, see Lissenden et al., 2007. The model did a very good job of predicting the variety of tests, particularly given the fact that only monotonic loading tests (tensile, creep, relaxation) and a single fully reversed cycle was used for characterization. It was particularly interesting that the model was capable of reasonably capturing the rate of accumulated strain during ratchetting under tensile mean stress. Given complex interrupted cyclic response, the model was able to both qualitatively and even quantitatively predict reasonably well both the cyclic and associated relaxation periods (in all quadrants of the stress-strain space) thus confirming the validity of the chosen functional forms for both hardening and thermal recovery. The quantitative inaccuracy is associated with the fact that the material specimens tested by Lissenden et al., 2007 was significantly “softer” than those tested by Castelli in Saleeb et al., 1994 which were used for characterization of the GVIPS model parameters.

results.title: Efficacy of Orion Flywheel Exercise Training in Ambulatory Subjects
results.abstract:
BACKGROUND  
The Orion Flywheel (OFW) is a novel spaceflight exercise device making its inaugural flight on Artemis II. Currently, the OFW is the sole aerobic and resistance exercise countermeasure system (CMS) for Artemis until the installation of the Gateway exercise device, after which it will continue to be relied upon during the critical lunar outbound and return transit phases of the mission. The OFW is a miniaturized, unpowered device that provides user-driven “iso-inertial” resistance through a single cable and a handlebar or harness interface. It is unknown whether the unique form and function of this device will be effective in supporting a comprehensive aerobic and resistance exercise intervention aimed at improving multi-system markers of health, fitness, and performance. The nature of isoinertial loads, having high eccentric loads which peak at the end of the eccentric phase, also poses questions as to the safety and subjective tolerability of completing 6 day/week of exclusively flywheel-type exercise. Previous investigations have not assessed flywheel exercise modalities as a stand-alone exercise system for providing concurrent aerobic and resistance exercise training at the doses planned per Artemis exercise requirements. Therefore, the purpose of this investigation is to understand whether the OFW is acceptable as a stand-alone exercise CMS for Artemis missions as currently planned by assessing changes to multi-system markers of physiological health, fitness, and functional task performance.

METHODS  
A structured and monitored exercise intervention will be used to evaluate changes in subjects’ multi-system health, fitness, and performance across an 8-week time frame in at least 15 healthy, free-living adults between the ages of 25-55. The intervention will consist of two 4-week cycles, with the first cycle following the planned exercise time for shorter-duration mission requirements (30 min/d, alternating between aerobic and resistance sessions) and the second increased to the exercise time planned for longer-duration missions (30 min/d aerobic alternating with 60 min/d resistance sessions). Aerobic exercise on the OFW will be performed in low gear using heart rate percentage targets and commonly employed aerobic exercise protocols for spaceflight. Resistance exercise will use the OFW medium and high gears with prescriptions following a progressive model based on established spaceflight periodization frameworks. Upon enrollment, all subjects will be familiarized with the testing procedures and with exercising on the OFW. Data collection will be completed at baseline prior to the first 4-week cycle, at the mid-point between the first and second cycles, and at post-intervention following completion of the second 4-week cycle. Metrics on exercise prescription adherence and subjective tolerance of the exercise loads will be tracked across subject participation. Outcome measures will include aerobic (cycle peak aerobic capacity, critical power) and full-body muscular performance (functional: countermovement jump, squat jump, depth jump, handgrip strength, YMCA bench press; isometrics: mid-thigh pull, leg press, bench press; isokinetic knee strength) measures to assess fitness, completion time of a simulated EVA task circuit (incapacitated crew rescue [sled drag], payload transport, prone recovery, traverse, sled push, Jacob’s ladder and overhead object lift) to assess functional performance. Additionally, blood markers and metabolic gas exchange will be collected concurrent with an acute bout of OFW exercise at baseline, mid and post timepoints to assess acute muscular and metabolic responses to flywheel training. Finally, immune markers will be collected to characterize [immune pathway activation responses] in relation to this Artemis-like exercise intervention.

RESULTS  
Data collection is expected to commence in June 2026 with the Flywheel exercise training to begin in July upon delivery of the OFW to the University of Houston – Clear Lake. 

SIGNIFICANCE  
By leveraging time available on this spaceflight Flywheel design to perform a controlled exercise intervention will provide critical insight into the ability of the OFW to preserve crew health and performance during exploration missions and will elucidate potential limitations with the device serving as a stand-alone exercise CMS capability. Findings will guide NASA’s human system risk recommendations for future lunar missions as well as recommendations for future Artemis CMS development and implementation plans.

results.title: Alternative Approach to Time-Delay Interferometry With Optical Frequency Comb
results.abstract: Spaceborne gravitational wave observatories, exemplified by the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) mission, are designed to remove laser noise and clock noise from interferometric phase measurements in post processing. The planned observatories will utilize electro-optic modulators (EOMs) to encode the onboard clock timing onto the beam phase. Recent research has demonstrated the advantage of introducing an optical frequency comb (OFC) in the metrology system with the modified framework of time-delay interferometry (TDI): the removal of the EOM and the simultaneous suppression of the stochastic jitter of the laser and the clock in the observation band. In this paper, we explore an alternative approach with the OFC-based metrology system. We report that after proper treatment, it is possible to use the measured carrier-carrier heterodyne frequencies to monitor the time derivative of the pseudoranges, which represent the physical light travel time and the clock difference. This approach does not require changing the existing TDI framework, as previous OFC based efforts did. Furthermore, this approach naturally captures not only stochastic jitter but also clock offsets and slow drifts. We also present the experimental demonstration of our scheme using two separate systems to model two spacecraft. Using this novel approach, we synchronize the two independent phase measurement systems with an accuracy better than 0.47 ns, while the stochastic jitter in the observation band is suppressed down to the setup sensitivity around the LISA performance levels at 15 pm/√Hz.

results.title: Design and Fabrication of a Microgravity-Capable Sanitization Unit
results.abstract: As NASA advances toward missions beyond low Earth orbit, ensuring food safety and cleanliness remains critical to protecting crew health. Current cleaning processes rely heavily on single‑use wipes for surfaces, tools, and edible commodities. For fresh crops grown on the International Space Station (ISS), previous crews have reported that the existing method, placing individual leaves in Ziploc bags and compressing them between ProSan‑soaked wipes, is time‑consuming and inefficient. This project seeks to reduce dependence on consumable cleaning supplies by developing a reusable device capable of washing tools and food items with water and/or approved sanitizers. The team has completed scaling analyses and fluid‑physics assessments to design and build a microgravity‑compatible spinning vessel (“salad spinner”) that enables controlled fluid introduction and removal. Engineering development also included structural integration for a parabolic flight requiring an aircraft‑mounted glovebox and a mechanism capable of achieving approximately 500 RPM to provide sufficient washing/rinsing of commodity test articles. A parabolic flight demonstration is planned for May 2026 to evaluate fluid injection, fluid dispersion, and debris/fluid removal performance using test articles such as radishes, tools, and small objects. Successful demonstration is expected to elevate the technology from its initial theoretical TRL-1 to TRL-5. This document summarizes all progress completed within the project’s defined performance period.

results.title: Combined Dual-Doppler and Polarimetric Radar Observations of Maritime Tropical Convection over the Western Pacific Ocean during the PISTON 2018 Campaign
results.abstract: Approximately four days (24-28 August) of shipborne dual-Doppler and polarimetric radar data were used to characterize the combined kinematic and precipitation structure of maritime tropical convection during the 2018 deployment of the Propagation of Intraseasonal Tropical Oscillations (PISTON) campaign. This period was not associated with active or suppressed Madden-Julian or Boreal Summer Intraseasonal Oscillations, thus serving as an exemplar of typical convection in this region, which heretofore has been only sparsely sampled (especially for vertical motion). A variety of convection was observed, ranging from shallow isolated cells to mesoscale convective systems, including some electrified storms as indicated by a global lightning detection network and a shipborne electric field meter. Convection with strong updrafts (> 5 m s-1) was rare but more likely to be associated with the presence of rimed ice and electrification. Updraft (downdraft) characteristic width and vertical depth were correlated with updraft (downdraft) speed, with coefficients ranging 0.55-0.60. From a composite perspective, updraft and downdraft widths were maximized in the mid-levels (6-10 km MSL), especially for the strongest vertical motions. Both upward and downward vertical mass transport rates were maximized near mid-levels. The median updraft lifetime (identified by cells with ≥ 2 m s-1) was only one radar volume (~7.5 minutes), with 83% of updrafts lasting less than 25 minutes. Columns of elevated differential reflectivity (≥ 1.5 dB) were most commonly found within ~3.5 km of updrafts. The observations were generally consistent with findings in similar regions across the globe.

results.title: Human System Performance Verification
results.abstract: BACKGROUND An important aspect of planning a verification Human-in-the-loop (HITL) test is determining the appropriate sample size needed for the test. While NASA requirements often specify number of subjects required for verification, several recent major spaceflight programs have approached NASA with a request to use fewer subjects to certify their spacecraft, and NASA management has agreed. The NASA Human Health and Performance subject matter expert (SME) community has serious concerns about this trend. Complicating this issue is the prevalence of sample size rules-of-thumb that give conflicting advice. Many guidelines pertaining to sample size exists in the literature, but it is not well understood how they apply to the HITL use case. There is little, if any, data pertaining to the effect on verification decisions. The main contribution of this project was to provide-NASA relevant data to help management better understand the risks related to the use of small sample sizes for verification testing. Additionally, we synthesized lessons learned from interview to understand previous decisions regarding the use of smaller than recommended sample sizes and b reviewing available rules-of-thumb for how well they apply to the verification use case. METHOD To characterize sample size rules-of-thumb, a literature review was conducted to identify well-known rules-of-thumb. These guidelines were then reviewed for applicability to verification testing by considering recommended user population, test type, stage of the design lifecycle etc. A study was conducted to collect evidence for assessing the impact of sample size on verification decisions. Participants (N = 49) completed one of two spacecraft verification scenarios, either executing a non-critical thruster burn, or responding to a system failure, on a high-fidelity spaceflight mockup. Data was analyzed to assess how increasing sample sizes affected verification decisions (e.g., true pass or false pass) relative to the full data set. SUMMARY Via interviews, it was found that many of the requests for smaller numbers of test subjects related more to timeline and resource conflicts than a direct desire for having fewer subjects. It was found that many of the rules-of-thumb available in the literature are not applicable to HITL verification tests due to specific context of use or because they are discussed outcomes not used in HITL verification tests. Study results demonstrated that the risk of making an incorrect verification decision is higher with fewer participants, and some test outcomes were more subject to incorrect decisions than others. While there is no magic number that will always lead to a correct decision these results indicate that a sample size of 10 to 15 is appropriate, and practical for HITL verification testing.
